summary: For ages 7–9: teach the inside of a volcano through a single labelled cutaway cross-section. Learners name the three parts (magma chamber, vent, crater), trace the path molten rock takes upward during an eruption, and grasp the load-bearing idea that magma and lava are the SAME hot melted rock — named by location (below ground vs above ground), not two different materials. Anchor on one image and one tracked blob of glowing rock whose NAME flips instantly as it crosses the surface, while its colour only cools gradually as the lava flows away.
misconceptions: Magma and lava are different substances (they are the same melted rock; the name changes at the surface).
Lava is fire, or the volcano is 'on fire' inside (it is glowing hot molten ROCK, not flame).
The vent is a bottomless hole straight to the Earth's core (it connects to a magma chamber, not the core).
A volcano is always a tall cone with a neat hole on top (shape varies; the crater is the surface opening).
The inside is hollow like a chimney (it is filled rock plumbing — chamber and vent — not an empty tube).

activities.title: Follow one glowing blob up the volcano
steps: Study a single labelled cutaway cross-section of a volcano, identifying the magma chamber, vent and crater on that one image before anything moves.
Build up pressure in the magma chamber and then release it, following ONE highlighted blob of glowing melted rock as it pushes up from the chamber, through the vent, and out of the crater.

Watch and say aloud what happens as the blob reaches the surface: the instant it comes out of the top of the vent into the open air (in the crater) its NAME changes from 'magma' to 'lava'. This is just a location rule, and the rock is still the same glowing-hot melt. Then watch the lava flow away from the vent and only GRADUALLY cool and darken, from glowing orange-white toward dark grey rock. It is the same stuff throughout: a new name straight away and a cooler colour later.
Tap each part (chamber, vent, crater) to pin its name as the blob passes it, so the anatomy is learned in the causal order of the eruption journey.
activities.insight: Magma and lava are one and the same melted rock; the name depends only on WHERE it is (underground = magma, surface = lava), and it changes the instant the rock crosses the surface. Freshly erupted lava is still glowing hot — it only cools and darkens over time. A volcano's interior is filled rock plumbing — a magma chamber connected by a vent to a crater opening — not a hollow tube or a path to the Earth's core.

activities.title: Label and reveal the cross-section
steps: On a static labelled cross-section, tap the magma chamber, vent and crater to reveal a short fact card for each.
Use a drill-down zoom into the magma chamber to see glowing melted rock held among hot rock (not an empty cave).
Answer a lift-the-flap at the crater rim: 'Is it magma or lava now, and why?'
activities.insight: The volcano's hidden interior can be made visible and named: chamber, vent, crater — with the magma chamber being molten rock within rock, and the crater being the surface opening.

activities.title: Consolidate the parts and the naming rule
steps: Drag labels onto a blank cross-section to place the magma chamber, vent and crater correctly.
Sequence the eruption journey in order: chamber → vent → crater.
Answer: 'The melted rock is now above ground — what do we call it?' and explain the reason in one sentence.
activities.insight: Learners can independently recall the anatomy and state the naming-by-location rule in their own words.

activities.title: Pressure-push model as a flagged analogy
steps: Watch or run a classic bicarbonate/vinegar reaction or a shaken fizzy-bottle release to feel how built-up pressure pushes material UP and out.
State explicitly how this model is and is NOT like a real volcano.
activities.insight: An eruption is driven by an upward push from built-up pressure — but the analogy is limited: the fizz is not real molten rock and not real heat.

checkQuestion: A child says the hot melted rock inside a volcano is called 'magma', and the stuff that pours out of the top is a totally different thing called 'lava'. Are magma and lava two different materials, or the same thing? Explain your answer.
checkAnswer: They're the SAME melted rock — the name just changes depending on where it is. Underground it's called magma; once it erupts out onto the surface it becomes lava. It travels up from the magma chamber, through the vent, and out of the crater.
